description: Anthropocene: a 6-member team from Chattogram, Bangladesh (computer science, architecture, EEE, marketing). For Field Shift we built Agrocene: a Bangla-first tool that replays 25 years of NASA POWER data against the crop rotations a farmer could plant, so they can see which ones came through the floods, droughts and heat. It works on cheap phones and by SMS.
summary: Agrocene is a Bangla-first decision-support tool that helps rice farmers in Bangladesh choose crop rotations for a changing climate. Its Rotation Lab replays what a farmer grows now beside real alternative rotations against 25 years of NASA POWER daily rainfall, temperature and soil-moisture data (2001–2025), for the flood-prone Sunamganj haor, the drought-prone Barind Tract and the salty Satkhira coast. In the haor, the usual long-duration boro rice was lost to flash floods in 5 of 25 years; a rice that leaves the field about three weeks sooner was lost once. Each option shows its year-by-year record, the water it needs, its effect on the soil, and what the model does not know, so farmers and the extension officers who advise them can weigh the choice against their own priorities. It runs on cheap phones, with a no-JavaScript Bangla page and an SMS-sized summary for phones without a browser.
details:
Live app: https://agrocene.vercel.app · Rotation Lab: https://agrocene.vercel.app/lab.html · Code (open source, MIT): https://github.com/ameerul-muminin/Hold-The-Field · 240-second video: https://youtu.be/Aai4bdT7et8

WHAT IT DOES

Field Shift asks for a tool that helps farmers compare crop rotations, including the existing one, and explains why each was suggested, the evidence, the benefits, the gaps, and what needs local review. Agrocene's Rotation Lab does exactly that for three Bangladeshi regions that face three different climate threats: flash floods in the Sunamganj haor, drought in the Barind Tract, and salinity on the Satkhira coast.

For each region it compares the most common existing rotation with documented alternatives. The rotations and their area shares come from the national cropping-pattern surveys published in the Bangladesh Rice Journal 21(2). Each rotation is replayed day by day against every year from 2001 to 2025 of NASA POWER data. The farmer sees:

- a strip of 25 squares, one per year: the crop came home, a thin year, or lost. This makes uncertainty visible instead of hiding it in an average;

- the water each crop needs beyond rain, bare-field days, and a soil-health indicator (legumes, crop diversity, ground cover, rooting depth);

- an evidence card with the five blocks the challenge asks for: why it was suggested, what the data shows, what it may offer, what we do not know (every unsourced value is shown as a gap, never filled in), and what to check locally before planting;

- a ranking that follows the farmer's own answers: soil type, whether they can irrigate, what they cannot sell or have no machine for, and what they fear most (losing the crop, low harvest, water cost, tired soil);

- a what-if slider for less rain or more heat, labelled as not a forecast.

Headline result: in the haor, the usual long-duration boro rice was lost to flash floods in 5 of 25 years (2004, 2010, 2016, 2017, 2022). A rice that leaves the field about three weeks sooner was lost once (2017). 2017 and 2022 match documented flash-flood years.

HOW IT WORKS

- Data: NASA POWER Daily API, community AG, at the farm point of each region and, for the haor, an upstream point in the Meghalaya hills, where the rain that causes haor flash floods falls. 9,131 days per region, no gaps.

- Crop water: FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration (Hargreaves method, from NASA daily max/min temperature), crop coefficients by growth stage, and a root-zone water store that starts each season from NASA root-zone soil wetness. Yield response to water shortage follows FAO-33/56.

- Heat: days above each crop's heat limit around flowering.

- Flood: a calibrated water-level model driven by three-day upstream NASA rainfall; the crop is lost after four days under water.

- Every crop parameter in data/crops.json carries a source link or is left empty and shown as a gap.

WHO IT IS FOR

Farmers, and the agricultural extension officers who advise them. The interface is in Bangla first (English as an option), works offline after loading, opens on low-cost Android phones, and has a no-JavaScript "lite" page. For phones with no browser, each region's finding fits in one SMS (a Bangla and a Latin-script version). A companion 3D game replays the real 2017 haor flash flood, so a farmer can feel why an earlier harvest matters before comparing rotations.

LIMITS WE STATE ON SCREEN

It is a simplified model on one 50 km NASA POWER grid cell per region, not a forecast. It has no market prices, salinity data or pest model yet, and soil water-holding values are estimates. It supports the farmer's judgement and tells them to ask their extension officer before changing crops.

NEXT

Salinity for the coast, more crops, field tests with haor farmers and extension officers, and more NASA datasets (MODIS vegetation, SMAP soil moisture).

TOOLS

JavaScript (ES modules, no build step), three.js, Python (standard library) for the NASA POWER download, Node's test runner (automated tests for the engine), Java 21 with LWJGL for the desktop edition, Vercel hosting, GitHub. The film's illustrations and animation were hand-drawn by the team.
